articles.title: American farmers are paying the price for US aid cuts halfway across the world
articles.summary: Extreme drought, cripplingly high prices for fuel and fertilizer, and the disruption of a market for surplus crops – America’s foreign food aid – have weakened the bottom line for many farmers.
articles.body: Jim Darnell’s family has been farming beans in Nebraska for three generations, but he says the past few years have been some of the more difficult for his crops and his sales. And the future, the 77-year-old said, also looks tough. “It’ll be a difficult time in farming for the next year,” Darnell told CNN. Farmers like Darnell in western Nebraska have suffered blow after blow in recent years. Extreme drought, cripplingly high prices for fuel and fertilizer, and the disruption of a market for surplus crops – America’s foreign food aid – have weakened the bottom line for his business, JD Farms. Washington’s funding cuts to food assistance programs and the abrupt dismantling of the US Agency for International Development early last year meant that farmers and crop elevators weren’t able to sell as much to aid programs like Food for Peace or the McGovern-Dole Food for Education Program, which feed millions globally. “Anytime we lose an end user, it eventually affects our prices… So, it did disrupt it for the price of beans,” Darnell said, adding that he is proud to contribute to any program that reduces global hunger. “That’s a great thing – any program that helps. And beans are a great thing to put in a program like that, because they’re great in protein and they store so well.” The United States has a long, bipartisan history of backing food assistance programs aimed both at helping domestic farmers and tackling global hunger. Food for Peace, which purchases agricultural products from American farmers each year to send to food-insecure populations overseas, has fed more than 4 billion people since it was created in the 1950s, according to the US State Department. “That’s a win-win for everybody,” said Cathy Kaufman, whose husband Mike runs a family farm that has been growing beans and corn for five generations. “It’s kind of amazing when you think that Nebraska farmers can help to achieve world security, as an end product, and feed the hungry.” But Congress recently cut government funding for Food for Peace by about 25%, from about $1.62 billion annually to $1.2 billion for FY2026. And the Trump administration has sent even less of that money out the door. The amount spent by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) on food aid commodities in 2025 and 2026 has fallen by about 55% compared to the spending levels in 2024 under the Biden administration, according to an analysis of USDA data conducted by the Center for Global Development (CGD). “The impact of this is playing out in human lives in the most catastrophic way imaginable,” said Sam Vigersky, an international affairs fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a New York-based think tank. “These are some of the most… impactful programs that the US government has anywhere in the world,” said Vigersky, who previously served as a senior humanitarian adviser to the US ambassador to the UN. “When you take money out of a program like Food for Peace, you’re taking food out of the mouth of starving children.” The White House originally proposed cutting the entire budget for Food for Peace and the McGovern-Dole International Food for Education program. But “Congress has really signaled continued support for food commodity programs,” according to Jocilyn Estes, a senior policy analyst at CGD. Food assistance programs have historically been protected by a bipartisan coalition of agricultural interests, shipping companies and humanitarian organizations. Experts have long noted that shipping bulk purchases of agricultural commodities overseas isn’t the most efficient way to administer humanitarian assistance, and in many cases, food could be purchased closer to crisis areas. “But right now, given the myriad of challenges and crises that the world’s most vulnerable populations are facing, I think any amount of bipartisan support for human care and assistance is good, and we should be really focusing in on how to improve that,” Estes told CNN. A spokesperson for the White House Office of Management and Budget told CNN that Food for Peace and McGovern-Dole are “inefficient, wasteful, and do not align with President Trump’s America First agenda,” and that they create “permanent dependency on the American taxpayer.” The budget preserves “far more efficient food aid programs,” the spokesperson added. The White House has called for cutting the funding, however, rather than redirecting it to other programs. Kaufman, who volunteers as an advocate for food assistance through the Christian nonprofit World Vision, said she believes cutting food aid programs not only threatens food security but also diminishes the United States’ global leadership. “Foreign assistance is less than 1% of our budget. I’m sorry, but that’s not going to balance our budget or even close,” Kaufman told CNN. “What it will do, though, is put our country in jeopardy of not being a world leader.” Revamped program drops countries at famine risk During the Trump administration’s dismantling of USAID, the Food for Peace program was transferred to the USDA. Some humanitarian experts have criticized that shift, arguing that the USDA lacks the same expertise in emergency management. The list of countries that the program supports has been heavily reworked under the USDA. Food for Peace provided American-grown food aid to seven non-emergency countries this year, while dropping several nations experiencing famine risk, like Somalia and South Sudan. “The administration has been clear that need is only one of the criteria, and that political objectives of the administration and the relationship with those governments is an important factor for them,” a senior official from a nonprofit told CNN, speaking anonymously because it still has US government contracts. “There are a lot of countries that are in need that, really, we’d like to see on that list.” In Yemen, which faces emergency levels of food insecurity after years of conflict, the Trump administration cut all foreign aid, including food assistance. Even still, farmers and agriculture industry workers told CNN that they applaud the USDA for its work picking up Food for Peace. Meanwhile, the senior nonprofit official told CNN that almost all its McGovern-Dole projects, which feed hungry schoolchildren overseas, were terminated in 2025, but “now some are coming back.” The official described the last two years as “unbelievably disruptive and confusing,” but added that the USDA has a “good team” working to resuscitate the work. The USDA declined to answer questions from CNN about Food for Peace but said in a recent statement that since the program was transferred “there has been over $1 billion invested in awards and agreements in principle for international emergency food assistance which utilizes approximately 467,000 metric tons of U.S. commodities.” Vigersky also noted that many countries are not only dealing with the end of Food for Peace deliveries but also facing cuts to other US aid programs plus cuts by other international donors. Grace Mavhezha, World Vision’s communications manager in Sudan, said “the funding uncertainty makes it increasingly difficult to maintain the planned scale of assistance.” The organization had to alter its food distribution plans and ration sizes this year due to funding reductions. She told CNN that “foreign food assistance is not simply about sending food overseas; it is about saving lives, protecting children, supporting families and giving vulnerable communities an opportunity to survive and recover from crises.” ‘Unbelievable need, globally’ American food companies and grain elevators up and down the country also play a role in food aid programs and are feeling the impacts of the aid cuts and last year’s sudden disruptions. Didion Inc., a family-run agricultural processing company in Wisconsin, told CNN that last year the supply chain was severely disrupted for its cereal product that’s used to treat acute malnutrition in young children overseas. The company had to suspend production, according to chief executive Riley Didion, but things have started moving again this year. “When that program stops, we also buy less corn from the farmers that are in our area,” Didion told CNN. “But the biggest impact by far will be people who don’t get fed.” Didion traveled to Kenya last October for meetings about improving the aid supply chain and the delivery of products to a refugee camp in Kakuma. “When I was there, there was a recent cut, and most of the folks were living off 30% or 40% of what they would normally get. That was really difficult to see,” he said. “There is an unbelievable need, globally.” He added that his firm is proud that its acute malnutrition products don’t bear the company’s own logo, but rather the American flag. “There’s an unbelievable gratitude that our team has the ability – and that our community has the ability – to play a part in feeding people all over the world.” CNN’s Becky Pinnington contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘Could you send me some nude photos?’: Soccer players accuse coach of abuse, urge FIFA to act in lightning rod case
articles.summary: Diego Guacci coached one of Argentina’s best known women’s soccer teams and the U15 and U17 national team. A new complaint from players has him back in the spotlight.
articles.body: As far back as she can remember, soccer player Florencia Mercau has supported one of Argentina’s best-known teams – River Plate. So when in 2014 the call came telling her she would be moving to Buenos Aires to join the club of her childhood heroes, Mercau was over the moon. For a young girl who grew up in a poor neighbourhood of Marquesado, in San Juan province, “it was the best thing I’ve ever been told,” Mercau said. “I’m a River fan. The chance to be at (Argentina’s) biggest club, and to know that, after the tough childhood I had, that I was able to reach River… It was my dream and I’ll give it my all.” But that dream quickly began to unravel, she said, when a week after she joined, age 20, she met the club’s recently hired new coach, Diego Guacci. “Not even a day had gone by and he sent me a text, addressing me as ‘Flor’ and saying, ‘Could you send me some nude photos,’” Mercau told CNN in an exclusive interview, the first time she has publicly discussed the abuse she says she endured. She says she deleted the texts and fought off Guacci’s advances, but that only provoked what she felt was a more dangerous version of him. “He’d come to me in practice and grab me from behind… he’d tell me, ‘delete the conversation, delete it because if you don’t, I will kill you and all your family,’” she said. “I didn’t even want to tell my mom because I thought it was wrong – I thought I was the one who was wrong.” Traumatized by the abuse, she said, but still wanting to play for the team she loved, Mercau found herself in an impossible position. One day, she said, she felt she could no longer continue. “In that moment I made the worst decision, I said I don’t want to live anymore, I don’t want to endure it anymore,” she said. “I don’t want to suffer anymore; I don’t deserve it because I always gave my best.” Mercau, now 32, survived the suicide attempt and is one of five Argentinian footballers to recently file a complaint with FIFA, soccer’s international governing body, against Diego Guacci. They accuse the former River Plate and Argentinian women’s national youth team coach of inappropriate conduct, including sexual harassment, threats and psychological abuse. But this isn’t the first time FIFA has been alerted to his alleged abuse. In 2020 and 2021, five other women filed a complaint alleging sexual harassment and psychological abuse, and even testified in an official FIFA investigation into Guacci. An investigatory committee recommended sanctioning him in 2021, but Guacci – who has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing – emerged from the ordeal mostly unscathed. “The Chamber believes that the evidence on file is insufficient to corroborate, to its comfortable satisfaction, the Players’ account of the events,” the adjudicatory chamber of FIFA’s Ethics Committee said in its findings. “Notwithstanding the above, the Chamber wished to stress that such conclusion shall not be considered as a recognition that the reported facts did not occur.” The decision left Guacci, who had moved on from River Plate to coach U15 and U17 women at the Argentinian national team, free to continue coaching, and the players in shock. It was “an absolute blow,” one of the players who filed the initial complaint, Gabriela Garton, told CNN. “If five players’ testimony is not enough, what do you need?” The new complaint has now fed into a political firestorm in Argentina, after Guacci’s wife, Andrea Guacci, brought further attention to the case by helping draft legislation that would increase jail time for those convicted of falsely accusing someone of a crime involving gender violence, sexual abuse, or crimes against minors. Critics say the legislation, which is expected to be voted on soon in the senate, is an alarming attempt to erode hard-won protections for women under a right-wing government which critics say has shown little concern for gender-based violence. Diego Guacci declined CNN’s request for an interview and did not respond to questions regarding the allegations against him, which he denies. The first investigation Garton, a former Argentinian national team player, was one of the first to file a complaint about Guacci’s behaviour, six years ago. Garton was 23 when she began playing for River Plate and had been at the club for a year when Guacci joined in 2014. Initially she had been excited to work with him, saying he seemed “really enthusiastic about women’s football” and appeared to want to “push the game forward.” But then Garton says the red flags started appearing. First, three or four players who’d worked with him before left the club, saying they “didn’t want to work with him,” she said. Months later she found out why. One of her teammates told her that Guacci had exposed himself to her, sending nude photos – and asking for nudes in return – and that player’s testimony was also part of the original FIFA investigation against Guacci. After that, Garton says she began to notice Guacci’s coercive behavior. One instance, after a difficult loss to rivals Boca Juniors, was so vile she still remembers it vividly, she said. “After the game, he said something along the lines of like, ‘if you girls play like that again, I’m going to put you all in the showers and… f**k you in the ass,’” Garton recalled. She too began thinking about leaving the club, while at the same time focusing on her call-up to the Argentinian women’s national team. That didn’t sit well with Guacci, she said. “He was saying that my behaviour was quite despicable, and that at the end of the day, I was like everyone else on the national team, willing to pull down my pants and be raped to be on the national team,” Garton said. Garton’s testimony became part of a FIFA investigation process that lasted roughly two years after soccer’s ruling body was first made aware of the allegations against Guacci in January 2020 and began a preliminary probe. FIFPRO, a global organization that represents professional soccer players, became involved the following month. By November 2020, FIFPRO had provided FIFA with a full report on behalf of four players, acting as legal representative for them. A fifth player came forward in 2021. “The investigation was almost non-existent. The procedure was extremely slow and sloppy,” FIFPRO’s senior legal counsel Alexandra Gómez Bruinewoud told CNN. FIFA launched formal investigation proceedings in April 2021 and invited Guacci to respond. In September of that year, he submitted a nine-page statement rejecting the accusations. Despite his rebuttal, the investigatory chamber found him to have breached several articles of FIFA’s Code of Ethics. It concluded that he sexually harassed one of the players and psychologically abused the others, recommending to the adjudicatory chamber that he be sanctioned. But that never happened. Soon afterwards, the three-man adjudicatory panel concluded there wasn’t enough evidence to impose any sort of sanction. “How many players need to present their testimony for a panel – a panel composed only of men – to decide that there was abuse?” Gómez Bruinewoud said. Guacci and his supporters, chief among them his wife Andrea, have publicly spun the outcome as an acquittal and launched a PR and legal campaign against the accusers, filing lawsuits against the five players and one journalist that became involved in the story. The same players and said journalist have also filed counter defamation claims against Guacci and those cases are still ongoing in Argentina. “It’s all lies, all lies,” Guacci repeatedly alleged in interviews on Argentinian television and social media segments, claiming the five players didn’t have the courage to show up for his hearing. “We were never invited to the hearing with the adjudicatory chamber,” Gómez Bruinewoud countered. “We found out there was a hearing with Guacci after it happened.” Adding to the players’ distress, Guacci also publicly named four of the women he believed were accusing him during the investigation. The players’ lawyers say FIFA then compounded the violation by publishing their initials in its final report, making their identification much easier. The outed players felt they had little choice but to publicly defend themselves in the face of a brutal smear campaign, which saw them attacked on social media by the Guaccis and their allies. The players and those who spoke out on their behalf say they were pressured and even threatened by Guacci’s supporters in a bid to make them walk back their accusations. Despite the pressure, Gabriela Garton, Luana Muñoz, Aldana Cometti and Camila Gómez Ares have maintained their version of events – the fifth player, known only as player E, has too, but decided to remain anonymous. CNN asked FIFA about the initial accusations against Guacci, and the fresh allegations put forward this year. Soccer’s governing body did not respond to questions sent by CNN, but defended its ruling and the procedures it has in place, saying it takes “any allegation of misconduct reported to it, including sexual abuse and harassment, extremely seriously and has a clear process in place.” It added that investigations follow the principle of due process, in accordance with its own code of ethics, guided by the law in Switzerland – where it is based – the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Arbitration for Sport. FIFA also did not confirm or deny it was looking into fresh allegations against Guacci, though insiders have told CNN it is normal for the organization not to disclose whether or not it has opened an investigation. Law on false accusations Although FIFA didn’t sanction Guacci, the Argentine Football Association (AFA) decided not to renew his contract. Guacci and his wife say the accusations against him destroyed his career and he has since moved to Italy. CNN was able to trace Guacci to a small town in central Italy. Two social media announcements from FC Fossacesia indicate he has been working with a youth team since July. The club confirmed Guacci had been volunteering with the team but provided no additional details. CNN reached out to Guacci and exchanged several emails with the former River Plate and Argentina manager over more than a month, submitting multiple requests for an interview. In his responses, Guacci repeatedly denied the allegations but declined to sit down for an interview or to answer any questions. Guacci claimed ongoing defamation lawsuits in Argentina prevented him from speaking publicly. Guacci has said in media appearances that he would like to resume his coaching career in Argentina, where the political climate has shifted under the right-wing government of President Javier Milei. Andrea Guacci has been a vocal advocate of the draft bill that would increase penalties for making false accusations of violence, proposed in 2024. She has presented her husband’s case as an example of a life forever damaged by what the couple say were false allegations against him. In Argentina, false accusations of gender-based violence account for a tiny fraction of complaints, according to a 2026 study by Argentina’s public prosecutor’s office. Andrea Guacci did not respond to CNN’s requests for comment. For Luana Muñoz, one of the five athletes who first filed the complaint against Guacci, the fact FIFA’s controversial decision is now being used by Andrea Guacci to promote this agenda is particularly worrying. “We started this to protect women, to protect kids, and it’s concerning because it will mean that they will take rights away from women,” Muñoz told CNN of the proposed bill, adding that it could make it even more difficult for victims of abuse to come forward. Both Muñoz and Garton said they were hopeful that with five more women coming forward in the new complaint against Guacci, soccer’s governing body would reopen the case. “You see women’s football and women’s rights in the world, how far we’ve come, but when things like this happen they kind of make you put your feet on the ground and understand there’s so much more that we have to fight for,” Muñoz said. Mercau has stayed out of the spotlight since her suicide attempt. But she told CNN that she too was committed to pursuing the case despite fears of retribution. “I’m scared to walk, I’m even scared to breathe,” she said. “But it’s that fear that won’t let me rest; that’s why I’m here today – so that all this can come to an end and I can get on with my life in peace.”

articles.title: Buffalo Bills outlast Kansas City Chiefs in defensive struggle to maintain top seed status in AFC
articles.summary: The Bills defense held Patrick Mahomes in check twice late, setting up a game-winning field goal to outlast the Kansas City Chiefs 13-10 on Thanksgiving.
articles.body: When NFL fans peeked at the Thanksgiving Day slate, their eyes likely focused on the night game between the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills. Two of the NFL's best passers going head-to-head with AFC bragging rights on the line. Many probably assumed this would be where all the offensive fireworks would be, but who knew the Turkey Day nightcap would be such a defensive struggle? CHIEFS AND BILLS TAKE CARE OF BUSINESS AHEAD OF THE NFL’S BIGGEST REGULAR-SEASON GAME The Bills outlasted the Chiefs 13-10 in what was by far the lowest scoring game of the three Thanksgiving showdowns on tap, keeping the top spot in the AFC and holding Kansas City at bay in the process. All of the storylines heading into this game were fixated on the quarterback duel between Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen, but it was the defenses that grabbed the headlines in primetime (though the inclement weather deserves some of the credit). CHIEFS' CHRIS JONES EXPLAINS WHY OPINIONS 'ARE LIKE BUTTHOLES' ON NATIONAL TELEVISION In particular, the Kansas City D was able to harass Allen, holding him to just 81 yards passing and forcing two interceptions. Most of Buffalo's damage came on the ground, though, as Allen and running back James Cook combined for 160 rushing yards, with the latter scoring the Bills' only touchdown of the game. The yardage numbers were rather paltry for both teams, with neither cracking the 250 yard mark, a far cry from the scoreboard light show viewers were treated to in the 1 o'clock and 4:30 games. The Chiefs won the turnover battle, forcing the two aforementioned Allen picks while keeping a clean sheet themselves. However, the Bills' defense and special teams each deserve their own set of flowers. The Buffalo D held the Chiefs and Mahomes to empty possessions twice in the final few minutes of the game, which in turn led to a nice punt return by Greg Dortch that would set up a short field for Tyler Bass's game-winning 57-yard field goal as time expired. For the Bills, this won't mean much in terms of their division standing. Buffalo is still running away with the AFC East and will likely face little resistance from the New England Patriots, who sit in a distant second at 4.5 games back as of Thursday evening. What this means for playoff seeding is a different ball game altogether. CALEB WILLIAMS' HEROICS HAVE BEARS THINKING NO. 1 SEED IN NFC PLAYOFFS Buffalo just took a huge step forward in locking up home-field advantage throughout the postseason, which also means they will get to face their playoff boogeymen in the friendly confines of Highmark Stadium. The Josh Allen era of the Buffalo Bills has been marred by an 0-3 record against the Chiefs in postseason play, with two of those losses coming in Kansas City. Getting a crack at their nemeses in their own backyard could be the difference between a trip to Southern California for the Super Bowl and sitting at home once again in late January, Thursday's win just made home cooking in the playoffs a possibility. articles.title: 'What is the need for a new Bill?' Congress slams BJP's 'amnesia' on women's Parliament quota
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday strongly criticised the BJP over its \"amnesia\" on Women’s Reservation Bill, questioning the delay over its implementation
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday strongly criticised the BJP over its "amnesia" on Women’s Reservation Bill, questioning the delay over its implementation and accusations of the being a roadblock.Congress leader P Chidambaram, targeted Union home minister Amit Shah over his remarks on the issue, saying he was either suffering from "amnesia" or being "economical with the truth".In a post on X, Chidambaram said the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, had already been enacted after the Bill was passed by both Houses of Parliament on September 20 and 21, 2023."Congress fully supported the passage of the Bill, and has been demanding the immediate implementation of the Act," he said.Questioning the government's delay, Chidambaram asked: "Why is the BJP government not implementing the Act?""What is the need for a new Bill?" he asked.Congress' general secretary in-charge Communications, Jairam Ramesh, also accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Shah of misleading the public over the purpose of the special session, alleging that the government was using the issue of women's reservation to divert attention from delimitation."Yet again, the mischievous PM-HM jodi is lying," Ramesh said in a post on X."The Special Session is thus NOT for women’s reservation. That is already a law which the PM-HM jodi have put into cold storage for over three years. The Special Session is for Delimitation," he added.Earlier, Shah said the government was commitment to implementing 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies, asserting that Rahul Gandhi would not be able to prevent its implementation.“The women of the country will certainly get 33% reservation of seats in the Parliament and state legislative assemblies,” Shah said. His remarks came ahead of the announcement of a three-day extended special session of Parliament, scheduled from November 30 to December 3."I want to tell Rahul Gandhi that it is our commitment that women of this country will get reservation (in Parliament and Legislative Assemblies). No one will be able to stop us," Shah later said.The Women's Reservation Bill was passed by Parliament in September 2023, providing for 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies. However, the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, made its implementation conditional on the publication of the first Census conducted after its commencement and a subsequent delimitation exercise to redraw constituencies.In April 2026, the government sought to amend this framework to bring the quota into effect ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha elections. Its proposed Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill also sought to increase the strength of the Lok Sabha from 543 to up to 850 seats and use the 2011 Census for delimitation.However, the Bill failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha. The Opposition supported women's reservation but objected to linking it with delimitation.Eight months after the defeat, the government is preparing to revive the proposals in the upcoming extended parliament session.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Gujarat ATS arrests suspected Jaish-e-Mohammed terrorist in Vadodara, recovers rifle and ammunition
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) has arrested a suspected Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) operative from Vadodara and recovered a rifle and more
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) has arrested a suspected Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) operative from Vadodara and recovered a rifle and more than 20 live cartridges from his possession, an ATS official said on Friday.The arrested accused has been identified as Md Saharul Islam, a resident of Assam, according to the official. A major operation by the ATS is currently underway, with further details awaited.The arrest comes amid heightened security operations against Pakistan-linked terror networks, particularly in Jammu and Kashmir, where security agencies are tracking an estimated 65 Pakistani terrorists operating across the Union Territory.Hunt on for 65 Pakistani terrorists in Jammu and KashmirAccording to officials in the security establishment, the presence of around 65 foreign terrorists has been confirmed through inputs from multiple intelligence agencies. Of these, 35 are believed to be affiliated with Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT), 25 with Jaish-e-Mohammed, while the remaining operatives are linked to other banned terror outfits.The latest assessment comes days after the killing of Lateef Bhat, described by security officials as the last known active local terrorist in the Kashmir Valley. He was killed in an encounter with security forces in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam district on November 18, following an eight-day search operation.Officials said the estimated number of active terrorists in the Union Territory has declined from 91 in 2024, which included both foreign and local militants, to around 65 at present, comprising only Pakistani nationals.The security agencies are monitoring the presence of these foreign terrorists in districts including Poonch, Rajouri, Kishtwar and Doda, particularly in remote areas with dense forests and mountainous terrain. Officials said the figures are based on assessments by multiple agencies and may fluctuate as terrorists frequently change locations.Security agencies intensify operationsThe changing security landscape in Jammu and Kashmir follows a sustained decline in the number of active local militants. However, officials said Pakistan-origin terrorists continue to operate in parts of the Jammu region, making counter-infiltration operations and intelligence gathering a priority.Addressing the passing-out parade of probationary deputy superintendents of police, sub-inspectors and assistant directors of the Forest Protection Force at the Sher-i-Kashmir Police Academy in Udhampur on November 18, Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha expressed confidence that Jammu and Kashmir would soon become terror-free. He also asserted that only a handful of foreign terrorists remained in the Union Territory.Security agencies have been conducting multi-agency operations based on intelligence inputs to track and neutralise these operatives. Earlier this year, security forces neutralised all seven members of a Jaish-e-Mohammed group led by Saifullah in Kishtwar.The group had infiltrated in April 2024 and was eliminated through a series of operations culminating on February 22 in the Chatroo area under Operation Trashi-I.Terrorist numbers decline over the yearsAccording to the available data, 135 terrorists were active in Jammu and Kashmir in 2022, including 85 foreign terrorists and 50 local militants. The number subsequently declined by nearly 48 in 2023, according to the figures provided.The reduction has been attributed to intensified counter-terrorism operations targeting active militants and their support networks.Despite the decline in local militant numbers, security agencies continue to focus on preventing cross-border infiltration, identifying logistical networks and tracking foreign terrorists operating in remote parts of the Union Territory.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: For much of the country, Thanksgiving featured nasty weather
articles.summary: Holiday storms flooded East Coast communities, knocked out power to nearly a million customers and prompted the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade.
articles.body: Holiday storms flooded East Coast communities, knocked out power to nearly a million customers and prompted the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade. High winds and flooding hammered both coasts, snarling holiday travel. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity Thursday evening, with the majority in East Coast states, according to the outage tracking website poweroutage.us. Over 2,200 flights to or from U.S. destinations were delayed and more than 400 were canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware. Macy’s postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade’s massive balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers. Windy rain sweeps the East Coast Torrential rain, high winds and flooding pounded sections of the East Coast. New Jersey was under a state of emergency, along with parts of New York. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England. Two people were rescued from their cars in New York City because of flooding, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday morning, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities. “There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said. The storms also flooded areas from North Carolina through New Jersey as high tide rolled in. Roads were closed, and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water. Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, Borough of Avalon Business Administrator Scott J. Wahl said. “Not quite Hurricane Sandy,” Wahl said of the benchmark storm for his village on the far south end of New Jersey’s Atlantic coast. Floodwaters washed debris over the road, and a few drivers were rescued after driving around barricades into floodwaters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said. Lance Miller, 54, said floodwaters in his Ocean City, New Jersey, neighborhood were about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest supermarket would probably “destroy your car.” Miller said he would be staying indoors and having Thanksgiving dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends were “not so lucky” and had flooding inside their homes. The Margate City Fire Department near Atlantic City, New Jersey, posted video on Facebook of water pouring through the city’s streets, even before heavy rains started. A firefighter said the tide was coming in ferociously, even with an hour to go before its peak. Water closed in on houses, and sandbags were piled in front of businesses. Some highways and bridges were temporarily closed. The nearly 18-mile (29-kilometer) Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel in southern Virginia was closed for several hours Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes and covered the two-lane highway. In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm. The storms also prompted several brief tornado warnings on Thursday, including a rare twister southeast of Seattle, Washington. President Donald Trump signed a disaster declaration Thursday for Florida in response to earlier flooding that damaged hundreds of homes and required water rescues. Trump had approved funding earlier this week, but gathered local officials on Thanksgiving to talk about it in a small signing ceremony at his home in West Palm Beach. Trump was asked about aid for Thursday’s storms on the East Coast. “Well, we’re going to look at that. We have some requests from others,” he said. Central states see snow; California faces floods Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St. Louis recording 7.3 inches (18.5 centimeters) of snowfall. Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, recorded 14 inches. The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 a.m., according to the city. Meanwhile, high-tide driven waves and strong winds caused flooding along the Pacific coast Thursday. The conditions were expected into Friday, according to the National Weather Service. Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles. King tides were surging along the West Coast. Video showed a massive wave tearing down part of the Pacifica pier in California on Wednesday, sending it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped pier in the summer after finding cracks. Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner posted more than a dozen itinerary changes on social media Thursday morning, starting with one that said trains could not run through San Clemente “due to track damage.” It also suspended service between Irvine and Oceanside because of washouts caused by high tide conditions. Service was further shut down from San Diego north to Oceanside and up to Los Angeles International Airport.

articles.title: Man pays Rs 2.17 lakh for fancy Haryana vehicle number, but SDM transfer stalls allotment; consumer court orders refund with interest and Rs 36,000 in compensation and costs after 90-day deadline lapses
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Haryana has directed the state Transport Department and the Regional Transport Office (RTO), Punhana, to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Haryana has directed the state Transport Department and the Regional Transport Office (RTO), Punhana, to refund Rs 2.17 lakh paid by a man for a fancy vehicle registration number after the authorities failed to assign it within the stipulated period due to the transfer of an SDM.The commission also awarded Rs 25,000 as compensation for mental agony and harassment and Rs 11,000 towards litigation expenses, holding the authorities liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.Why was the man's fancy registration number cancelled?The complainant, Hari Chand Lather, a resident of Karnal, had participated in an online auction conducted by the Haryana Transport Department and won the bid for registration number HR93D0002 on November 22, 2024, according to the court order.Also read: Bharat Gas distributor told to restore man's LPG connection, pay Rs 20,000 in reliefHe paid Rs 2.17 lakh through two transactions: Rs 31,000 as earnest money on November 17, 2024, and Rs 1.86 lakh after winning the bid on November 22, 2024. The department issued an allotment letter stating that the number had to be assigned to an eligible vehicle within 90 days, failing which the allotment would automatically stand cancelled without a refund.Lather approached the RTA/RLA office in Punhana on February 17, 2025, four to five days before the deadline, with the required documents. However, a staff member allegedly told him that no work would be done until the new SDM took charge following the transfer of the existing SDM.As the 90-day period expired, the allotment was cancelled. Lather said he had recorded the conversation with the staff member and repeatedly requested the authorities to assign the number. He approached the commission seeking a refund of Rs 2.17 lakh with 13% annual interest and Rs 30,000 as costs.The Transport Department and RTO did not appear despite receiving notices and were proceeded against ex parte.What did the commission say?The bench comprising president Jaswant Singh and members Neeru Agarwal and Sarvjeet Kaur observed that the complainant had approached the authorities within the stipulated 90-day period but they failed to assign the registration number because of the transfer of the SDM."Thus, it has been proved on record, complainant approached the OPs within stipulated period of 90 days for assigning of the registration mark on his vehicle but OPs failed to assign the said registration number on the lame excuse of transfer of SDM Punhana, which is not justified in the eyes of law," the commission observed.It further held that the authorities were responsible for either assigning the registration number or refunding the deposited amount of Rs 2.17 lakh."Thus, it was the duty of the OPs either to assign the abovesaid registration number to the complainant or to refund the deposited amount of Rs.2,17,000/- but OPs failed to do so. Hence, the act of the OPs amounts to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice," the bench concluded.Final orderAnnounced on November 3, 2026, the commission allowed the complaint and directed the authorities to:Refund Rs 2.17 lakh with 9 percent annual interest from the date of deposit until realisation.Pay Rs 25,000 as compensation for mental pain, agony and harassment.Pay Rs 11,000 towards litigation expenses.The authorities must comply with the directions within 45 days of receiving a copy of the order.

articles.title: Venezuela to scrap law that bars opposition from public office
articles.summary: The legislation has been criticised for enabling political persecution since it was introduced two years ago.
articles.body:
Venezuela will repeal a law that bars opposition figures from assuming public office, the speaker of the National Assembly Jorge Rodríguez has said.

The legislation, which was introduced two years ago, has been criticised for enabling political persecution, but Rodríguez said no politician had been subjected to its provisions.

The older brother of Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodríguez said he expected the reforms to be approved next week.

Delcy Rodríguez's interim government has been negotiating with opposition parties since taking over at the start of the year, when former President Nicolás Maduro was seized by the United States.

The legislation, known as the Simón Bolívar Law, was passed shortly after the election in July 2024 in which then-incumbent Maduro was declared the winner amid widespread allegations of fraud.

Under the legislation, individuals who requested or supported foreign sanctions against Venezuela were permanently banned from political office and had their assets confiscated.

"Legislative processes are dynamic processes. That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through," Jorge Rodríguez said.

During subsequent talks, which began in August, the interim government and parts of the opposition agreed to review several other laws as part of a "route map towards democracy", according to an opposition statement.

Delcy Rodríguez has promised that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election despite being excluded from transition talks.

Machado returned to the country in October after more than 10 months in exile.

In the 2024 election, Machado's ally Edmundo González ran in her place after she was barred from running for office by Maduro's government.

The electoral authority, which was closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.

The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.

articles.title: Erin Patterson: Mushroom murderer launches last-ditch High Court appeal
articles.summary: Erin Patterson is serving life in prison for poisoning his relatives with a toxic mushroom lunch in 2023.
articles.body:
Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.

Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".

She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.

Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.

She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.

Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.

He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.

She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.

Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

articles.title: Huntingdon train attack survivor praises man who saved her during stabbings
articles.summary: Astrid credits Stephen Crean with saving her life during the Huntingdon train attack last year.
articles.body:
A student who survived the Huntingdon train attack has met for the first time with the passenger she believes saved her life during the stabbings.

Astrid told BBC News that Stephen Crean's decision to confront Anthony Williams gave her time to escape. "I owe him my life," she said.

Williams was found guilty on Thursday of attempting to murder Crean and 13 others .

The then 19-year-old and 61-year-old Crean were just strangers on a train when she ran down the carriage screaming that there was a man with a knife.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Crean ran towards Williams and was stabbed in the hands, back and neck. She was the last person to reach the buffet car and believes his actions gave her time to get in and shut the door.

Violent knifeman told doctor his psychosis drugs weren't working days before train attack

How the Huntingdon train attack unfolded - carriage by carriage

Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.

Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."

Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."

Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.

"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."

She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.

"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.

Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.

"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.

During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.

He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.

The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.

"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."

Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.

Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.

Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.

On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.

As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."

Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.

She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

articles.title: Devon hotels' late season boost from Turkey and Tinsel holidays
articles.summary: Hotels get a significant seasonal boost from coach trippers getting an early taste of Christmas.
articles.body:
Coach trippers visiting the South West to stay in hotels for Christmas themed breaks in November and December contribute millions to the local economy.

So-called tinsel and turkey holidays have been running for decades, bringing much needed income to the hospitality sector at what can be a quiet time of year.

The English Riviera Bid company says during November and December, 400,000 people stay in Torbay contributing £30m to the local economy.

The Caledonian Torbay Hotel in Torquay's hotel manager Pedro Anzules said: "I've been doing this myself for over 25 years and it has always been really attractive. It's still a thing, it's just amazing."

The hotel hosts about 150 guests each week at this time of year, most of whom have travelled by coach from the north of England.

It is a four day break, recreating Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Years Eve and New Years Day.

Tickets for turkey and tinsel tours can cost between about £250 and £550, depending on the hotel and where the trip originates.

The Portbyhan Hotel in Looe, Cornwall said it was welcoming about 20 tours over the season, bringing more than 600 guests to the town.

"People want to enjoy the Christmas, people want to see Father Christmas," Anzules said.

Sisters Lorraine Beverley and Lesley Hart from Yorkshire have taken regular coach trips for 14 years, and are staying at the Caledonian Torbay on their first tinsel and turkey experience.

"It's just such a good atmosphere and the people that come on the coaches, they're just out for a good time," Beverley said.

"When you see some of the older people in their 80s enjoying themselves and getting up dancing, it's lovely."

"As I say it's been so friendly, and it is as soon as you get on the coach as well," she added.

Hart said: "When you get here, the hotel and the staff can't do enough for you, and Santa is absolutely brilliant."

Majestic Coaches in Teignmouth, said it was behind the original turkey and tinsel tours in the 1990s. These days it runs festive tours to places including Torquay, Blackpool, Scarborough and Eastbourne.

Mark Wright, director at the company, said: "I think it was the saviour of a lot of seaside holiday resort hotels across the country that used to lay off staff in November, December. And it's a great success."

He said the the firm was the first to offer the trips and at one stage ran them for six months, starting in September and running until Valentine's Day.

"It's now reduced to three months because there's more hotels doing it, so it thins the market a bit. But we still start in last week of October and we go through it till last week of January.

"So we're definitely the originators. And we still like to think we're the best. I'm sure there's competition out there, but we are good."

The English Riviera BID company sees the tours as an important way of extending the season by keeping bars and restaurants open, and maintaining employment for local people and supporting local suppliers.

It said they make a large contribution to the visitor spend for November and December, which is worth more than £30m.

"A lot of the clientele are probably 60 plus and enjoy social holidays together, " said Carolyn Custerson from the organisation.

"This brings people together as a group to have a jolly time, enjoying traditional festivities.

"Maybe many of them live on their own, and come away and be part of a group like this and having fun in what is traditionally a miserable time of the year with weather in November and December.

Lindsey Bailey-Lewis, general manager of The Portbyhan Hotel in Looe said: "Turkey and tinsel coach tours are an important part of our winter season and something we're pleased to welcome at the hotel."

Guests have breakfast and evening meals included and receive a Christmas gift to take home.

She said: "Looe has so much to offer during the season and its wonderful to show off the town to our guests.

"There's a lovely atmosphere when the groups are here and we love to welcome repeat customers as well as new faces."

Tours to the hotel are organised by Belle Coaches, based in Lowestoft, Suffolk.

Beth Sissen, tours manager, said customers "absolutely love these breaks" which sometimes begin in late October.

"Some of our customers will travel on more than one turkey and tinsel break each year, and they travel year after year, providing sometimes lonely people with company in what can be a difficult time of year for them if they don't have many family or friends around them, especially as the nights draw in and it's cold and dreary outside.

"These breaks work so well for both us and the hotels, to make sure we are still able to provide people with holidays and keep business running when it's not the traditional time of year to go on holiday - when it's not warm outside and most attractions have closed for winter."

articles.title: Malaysia: Six charged for trafficking drugs at military air base
articles.summary: Authorities are uncovering the true scale of alleged years-long drug smuggling involving Malaysia's air force.
articles.body:
A Malaysian court has charged six people, including three Malaysian military personnel, for trafficking drugs at an air base near the capital Kuala Lumpur, local media report.

Authorities say they are working to uncover the scale of suspected years-long drug smuggling involving Malaysia's air force. At least three tonnes of drugs are believed to have been trafficked across air bases since August 2024.

The suspects charged on Friday are among 13 who were arrested earlier this month, after authorities seized 96.64kg of methamphetamine, a highly-adictive synthetic drug, at Subang Air Base.

If convicted, they could be sentenced to death or life imprisonment.

The drugs, concealed in five suitcases and a box, were discovered at Subang Air Base during a routine inspection.

Besides the six suspects who were charged on Friday, there are seven others - four air force personnel and three civilians - who were arrested but have not been charged.

One of the suspects was an air force pilot who coordinated and transported drugs from peninsular Malaysia to Sabah, a Malaysian state on the island of Borneo, police said.

This is just the tip of what authorities allege are years-long drug trafficking operations involving its air force.

Authorities have identified 21 cases of drug smuggling involving air force infrastructure, dating back to August 2024, Malaysia's interior minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail told parliament on Thursday.

He said the drugs, which weighed a total of three tonnes, were valued at 156 million Malaysian ringgit ($37.9m; £28.9m).

"Had we not dismantled this operation, millions of people would have fallen victim," he said according to local media.

"This is not merely a serious criminal offence as it also threatens the integrity of our security and defence institutions."

Saifuddin Nasution said authorities would expand the investigation to uncover the full scale of the syndicate.

While they have identified the suspected leader of the syndicate, they have not made an arrest, he said.

Established in the 1980s, Subang Air Base is a military airport located near the capital Kuala Lumpur. It is often used for receiving foreign dignitaries visiting Malaysia. In 2024, it was also where more than 100 Palestinians, injured and evacuated from Israel's war on Gaza, arrived for medical treatment.

articles.title: ‘You can’t stop it’: Indians embrace Pakistani dramas, defying bans
articles.summary: India has tried to keep Pakistani dramas off its screens since May 2025. But Indians can’t get enough of these shows.
articles.body:
When New Delhi-based cultural impresario and curator Abu Sufiyan Khan organised a recent screening of the Pakistani romantic drama Dar-e-Nijaat in the Indian capital, he was stunned. It was meant to be a private event for 45 people, at most. Khan got more than 700 requests for attendance.

Like all other Pakistani shows and songs, Dar-e-Nijaat is officially banned in India. Yet every weekend, Indian viewers gather on Instagram to exchange clips, debate episodes and celebrate its leading character, Abu Bakr.

Offline, watch parties and group screenings are organised in different parts of the country. As the craze for the show – which involves a young woman Zaryab, her childhood love Zamil, and Abu Bakr, who later steps into Zaryab’s life to fill a void – has gripped Indian cities, the police have been left playing cat-and-mouse.

At least two screenings in the southern city of Bengaluru, scheduled for this coming weekend, have now been cancelled after authorities saw posters advertising the events. But those attempts at a crackdown haven’t dimmed the appeal of the show.

One phrase, repeated across fan pages and comment sections, has become a shorthand for its craze: “Sabr ka phal nahi, Abu Bakr chahiye,” (We don’t want the reward of patience; we want Abu Bakr.)

It is a playful twist on a familiar Urdu proverb, and an indication of the affection Indian viewers have developed for a fictional Pakistani man. “We have all been looking forward to an Abu Bakr. I have been going gaga over him because of how empathetic he is, and that is what is missing in most of the men these days,” says Rakhshanda Mujib, a fan from Bengaluru.

Yet the excitement over Dar-e-Nijaat is only the latest expression of a much wider appetite. India’s efforts to keep Pakistani entertainment off its screens have done little to extinguish the appetite for it.

“Indians cannot approach Pakistani artists on Instagram, access Pakistani music on Spotify or view Pakistani dramas without VPNs or proxies on YouTube,” Sufiyan Khan said.

But for many, the forbidden fruit of Pakistani culture remains alluring enough to risk breaching the official ban.

Despite multiple wars and near-perpetual tensions, India and Pakistan had for decades allowed cultural exchanges – even though they each periodically imposed restrictions.

But informal bans on Pakistani artistes working or performing in India gained ground over the past decade as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in New Delhi increasingly dialled down all contact with Pakistan to a bare minimum.

A new tipping point arrived in April 2025, when gunmen killed 26 tourists in Pahalgam, in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan for the attack, while Islamabad denied any role. The neighbours fought an intense four-day war before agreeing to a ceasefire.

Since then, India has banned all Pakistani songs, movies and dramas from streaming platforms, including YouTube. It has cited national security for its decision. This week, it demanded that Netflix take down – from viewing in India – Pakistan’s first show on that platform.

Yet while China imposed a similar ban on Korean pop culture in 2016, and it held for the better part of a decade, India’s efforts appear to be failing.

The reason lies in where the chokepoint sits. China controls the platforms its citizens use. India does not control YouTube. Section 69A of India’s Information Technology Act lets the government direct platforms to block content, and the orders are generally confidential. In practice, YouTube geo-blocked Pakistani channels for users in India.

But a geo-block governs a platform, not a viewer. A VPN changes where a viewer appears to be, and anyone who downloads a drama that way can re-upload it from an account inside India.

On May 8, 2025 – the day streaming platforms were told to drop Pakistani content – searches for VPNs in India rose 72 percent, according to the monitoring firm Top10VPN, which links the rise to both governments blocking each other’s online content.

Those VPNs downloaded in India translate into good business for Pakistani channels like ARY Digital, the network behind Dar-e-Nijaat.

“Indian viewers account for 30 to 35 percent of total views for Pakistani channels”, says Jerjees Seja, head of ARY Entertainment. “In this day and age, you can make access to content difficult, but you can’t stop it.”

Seja’s assertion is hard to dispute. The 2022 drama Tere Bin and the 2024 soap Kabhi Main Kabhi Tum were both also wildly popular in India. Pakistani director Mehreen Jabbar says viewers in India message her about her series such as Dr Bahu, Jackson Heights and Daam.

So, what makes these shows click for Indian audiences?

Culturally, the similarities between India and Pakistan mean that a lot that’s seen in Pakistani shows is instantly relatable for many across the border. Seja adds that Pakistan’s entertainment industry has also grown in its quality of production. “Our content has become very strong over the years,” he said. “It is realistic, on-the-ground, thought-provoking, and relatable.”

But there’s another reason, too, suggests Sufiyan Khan, that dramas like Dar-e-Nijaat find a willing audience in India. Far too often, Indian shows and movies stereotype Muslim characters. By contrast, Dar-e-Nijaat’s appeal, he said, lies in part in its “exceptional portrayal of Islam as not being threatening or Bollywood-style performative with kohl eyes and prayer caps but a refreshing, non-judgmental and inclusive Islam where all the rituals are being practised with humility”.

Culture is inconvenient in wartime politics because it makes an enemy familiar. But technology has made it harder for governments to firewall entire societies.

“Over the last few years, a whole wave of Indian people are consuming Pakistani TV shows, music and influencer content. There has been a democratisation of culture and access, which has led to the breaking of stereotypes,” said Aishwarya Verma, a policy analyst in Delhi. “Back in the day, we didn’t know too much about our brothers and sisters across the border, and vice versa.”

Pakistani actress and singer Haniya Aamer, for instance, is popular for her music in India. A recent song by her, Pablo, features Indian actress Rakhi Sawant. “We’re all listening to her music,” said Verma. “Who would have thought?”

Ajay Bisaria, former Indian high commissioner to Pakistan, said bans of the kind India has imposed rarely work. “Technology changes. It makes both borders and bans less relevant. Governments impose bans because culture is visible and easy to restrict. Pakistan has done the same: Indian films were banned there for decades.”

Yet, as with Pakistani shows in India, Bollywood thrived on pirated cassettes in Pakistan.

“Culture”, Bisaria said, “has played a massive binding force in the bilateral relationship between India and Pakistan, whether the two nations have wanted it or not.” And Dar-e-Nijaat shows it continues to do so.

articles.title: Betsi Cadwaladr CEO pulls out of new post after damning review
articles.summary: Carol Shillabeer had been due to take up a new post at a health board in north west England in 2027.
articles.body:
The chief executive of Wales's largest health board will no longer take up a new post in England, following a damning review of her current organisation's leadership.

Carol Shillabeer, who has been Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board's chief executive since May 2023, had been due to lead the Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Trust in England in the new year.

But a review into the Welsh health board found that, in some parts, targets and money had a "greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care".

The Lancashire and South Cumbria Trust said the "seriousness of the findings" could not be ignored and Shillabeer made the "personal decision" to withdraw from the role.

Dyfed Edwards, chair of Betsi Cadwaladr health board, confirmed Shillabeer would leave her current post on 3 January 2027. He thanked her for her service and wished her well for the future.

Confirming Shillabeer's withdrawal from the role, the Lancashire and South Cumbria Trust said it had "taken our time to carefully consider the situation and discuss the matter" with her.

"Carol feels that this is the best course of action for the sake of the patients, our communities, and LSCFT staff."

"We agree with her decision and wish her the best for the future," it added.

A spokesperson said that a board of trustees would consider the next steps regarding the appointment of a new chief executive.

Shillabeer spent three and a half years leading the health board, which covers all of north Wales. She was appointed after the Welsh government put it into "special measures" for the second time in its history.

It has been under the highest level of oversight due to concerns about care quality, patient safety and leadership .

The independent review published on Tuesday found the health board lacked "the organisational conditions necessary to reliably deliver and sustain improvement".

It concluded that senior leadership was "immature and ineffective", with weak senior management putting the quality of patient care at risk.

It also said the health board had a "dedicated and loyal" workforce, with a "high level of expertise" across many services, as well as the capacity to provide strong local services.

The health board apologised and said it now needed to concentrate on improving its leadership and allowing its staff to "flourish".

Responding to the document, Health Minister, Mabon ap Gwynfor MS, rejected calls for "radical action or structural change".

Instead, he suggested that "stability" is needed following a period characterised by "too much change."
