articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries has disarmed a progressive revolt, but can he deliver?
articles.summary: The presumptive House speaker’s political pragmatism will be tested by divisions over healthcare, Israel and Iran.
articles.body:
The overwhelming blue wave of the 2026 United States midterm elections should have simply been seen as a crowning achievement for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries that propelled him into the position of next speaker of the House of Representatives. And while that outcome appears all but guaranteed now that he has secured more than enough support from the incoming House Democratic Caucus, Jeffries’ ascent to the top House leadership position has been significantly rockier than anticipated.

The blue wave was, in part, a progressive and anti-establishment phenomenon. And while we in the media have likely exaggerated the impact of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in this year’s election cycle, DSA-affiliated and other newly elected far-left lawmakers have already asserted themselves as a vocal minority amongst the incoming House Democratic Caucus. They’ve done so by calling on the party to move left on issues such as healthcare, campaign finance and America’s relationship with Israel. And these newly elected progressives have also targeted congressional leaders, namely Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who they see as embodying the party’s status quo.

Jeffries has reached the pinnacle of power within his party by being a shrewd political operator who has deftly managed the leverage of the Democratic minority in the closely divided House. His handling of the recent challenge to his leadership shows that he remains a step ahead of his opponents within the party. Jeffries declined the opportunity to be chosen by acclamation, an option that could have allowed him to gloss over the opposition to his speakership. Instead, Jeffries insisted on a formal secret ballot. The choice was strategic. Much like a prime minister calling for early elections, he organised the vote to happen before progressive opposition had coalesced around a single candidate (unlike in the Senate, where Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen is amassing support to challenge Schumer). The move represented a tactic Jeffries observed while under the wing of Nancy Pelosi, who called a similar vote in 2018 after her leadership was challenged by vocal incoming members of Congress. In the end, potential challengers for the role of speaker, such as Representatives Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, declined to throw their hats in the ring to run against Jeffries. The vast majority of the caucus fell in line behind the New York congressman, with 251 votes in favour and only 11 against, the latter largely from incoming DSA-aligned representatives-elect.

For Jeffries, the progressive revolt against his leadership has been, in the short term, a mere speed bump on his path to becoming speaker. In the longer term, those 11 “no” votes represent a more significant progressive challenge to Jeffries’ record and agenda that will not easily disappear. However, the presumptive next speaker of the House is poised to overcome this challenge, as his skill as a political operative, the relatively weak position of his progressive opposition, and the historic nature of Jeffries’ leadership all work in his favour.

Over the course of the 2026 election cycle, Jeffries secured the support of important progressive figures, including fellow New Yorkers such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. During the brief post-election speculation over his leadership, the New York congressman also won over progressives including Texas Representative Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Jeffries’ predecessor as Democratic leader, Pelosi, was able to manage dissent from the progressive Squad through a combination of personal relationships and strategic committee assignments that channelled their energies toward oversight of the executive branch. Jeffries may likewise seek to manage the “Bloc”, as the new progressives are being called by some, in similar fashion.

Meanwhile, Jeffries’ primary message since the midterm elections has been one of affordability, a potent message that has resonated with voters across the political spectrum and thus can unite centrists and progressives within the Democratic Party. The speaker-designate has also signalled that he is willing to move in the direction of progressives’ concerns on substantive issues. Most notably, on November 17, the eve of the speaker nomination vote, Jeffries endorsed a plan to expand Medicare by lowering the age of eligibility for older Americans, covering children under 18, and including dental, vision and hearing coverage. This new “Medicare for more” plan, coupled with rolling back Trump-era cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits, has been gaining steam among both centrists and progressives. The latter have framed it as a quickly achievable first step towards Medicare for All. Both progressive elder statesman Senator Bernie Sanders and members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus have adopted this rhetoric.

Whether this “first step” framing is accurate is unknowable. The Affordable Care Act was presented in similar terms, but the progressive aim to use Obamacare as a foundation to build a universal healthcare system did not materialise over the subsequent decade. However, the willingness of major progressive forces to adopt the narrative seems to be opening space for Jeffries to navigate. This undercuts the power that the incoming progressives have to make healthcare a major dividing issue within the Democratic caucus.

Jeffries also has the power of history on his side. The congressman from Brooklyn is poised to take control of the top House spot as the chamber’s first Black speaker. He will be backed by an unprecedented slate of diverse leaders within the Democratic House Caucus, with historic firsts for Black, Hispanic and Asian legislators, among others. Even President Donald Trump acknowledged Jeffries’ personal acumen and the historic nature of becoming the first Black speaker, calling it “a big deal”, and referring to Jeffries as “a very smart guy”. Jeffries has in turn signalled a willingness to work with members of the Trump administration, though not with new White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, who Jeffries calls a “stone-cold racist”.

Black candidates and Black voters played huge roles in Democrats’ 2026 surge in ways that have not neatly mapped onto the “centrist insiders v. progressive outsiders” narrative that has defined the party’s main internal division. Though Black Democrats and progressives are by no means mutually exclusive wings of the party, the far left has sometimes had difficulties appealing to Black voters. As such, progressives face potential backlash if they are perceived as attempting to prevent or hamstring the leadership of the first Black speaker of the House. Already, some of the attacks against Jeffries have been condemned for racist language and undertones. Progressives run the risk of being tone-deaf and appearing on the wrong side of history, meaning that they will have to tread lightly if they continue to question Jeffries’ leadership.

In the short run, Jeffries has made the right moves politically and leaned into the importance of the moment, all while solidifying his coalition and moving leftward in a way that balances progressive priorities with legislative practicality. Whether he can temper progressive demands and maintain a unified caucus may depend on forces outside of his control. In terms of Democrats’ domestic agenda, incoming Senate sensation and Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is becoming the face of the Medicare for All movement, even pushing for a long-shot deal with President Trump on the issue. Growing momentum within the Senate could push the issue beyond Jeffries’ ability to manage. Similarly, in a recent New York Times interview, Jeffries signalled a willingness to walk a tightrope between holding the Trump administration accountable and working with the White House and other Republicans. But this balancing act may prove untenable if the continued lawlessness of Trump and his cabinet leads to intensified demands for investigations and even impeachments.

And foreign affairs may be an even larger stumbling block for Jeffries, who has come under fire for his support for Israel as sentiment grows in both parties to re-evaluate the US relationship with its longtime Middle East ally. For now, Jeffries has gotten some cover by gaining the support of figures like Mamdani, a vocal and credible critic of the genocidal war in Gaza and of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians. But in that same New York Times interview, Jeffries prevaricated when asked about accepting AIPAC funding in the future or pushing for legislation that would cut weapons sales to Israel and impose sanctions on entities tied to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Again, Jeffries appears to be offering a compromise, promoting the less forceful West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act, which targets the sponsors of settler pogroms but not the underlying scheme of settlement itself in Palestinian territory. It’s less clear that such a stance will be enough to satisfy Jeffries’ left flank. However, the growing controversy over AIPAC led the pro-Israel lobbying group, even prior to November’s election results, to shift its strategy of supporting candidates to a model that emphasises individual donors rather than direct political action committee funding for campaigns. The electoral shellacking that AIPAC-backed candidates experienced in the midterm elections may further lead the lobbying organisation to take a less high-profile approach going forward, which could help to slightly tone down Israel’s prominence in US politics.

For the time being, the Iran war is the more pressing foreign policy concern, and this will be one of Jeffries’ first major tests. He has pledged to prioritise ending the war, a popular stance that could be another unifying position for centrists, progressives and even some Republican lawmakers. But the speaker-designate has already been criticised for indicating that he might be willing to cut a temporary budget deal with Republicans that keeps money flowing to the war rather than using the leverage of a government shutdown to insist on cutting funds for the conflict. Even Trump and Vice President JD Vance have acknowledged the Iran war as a major reason behind Republicans’ 2026 defeats. Failure by Jeffries to take bold action against the conflict now will be seen as a missed opportunity and create a new opening for progressives to question his fitness to lead in this moment.

After securing the nomination for speaker, Jeffries surprised the incoming Democratic House caucus with a visit by former President Barack Obama, to whom Jeffries has been compared before. Obama was a unique leader who combined a principled pragmatism with an unmatched ability to inspire, and he urged the new Democratic representatives to stick to their principles while learning how to “get s*** done” with colleagues who had different points of view. Jeffries leans more toward Obama’s pragmatism than his idealism, and his penchant for practicality at the expense of vision may be the presumptive speaker’s greatest strength and biggest liability. Even if he is willing to compromise with the left wing of his party, Jeffries will not be the bold visionary that progressives want leading the House. But with domestic and foreign concerns to address such as healthcare and the war with Iran, Jeffries has the chance to be the leader who gets things done. Jeffries will have the next two years to accomplish these and other goals for the party and its supporters. Whether or not he delivers results on these issues, and how voters assess the party’s performance come 2028, will make or break Jeffries’ speakership.

articles.title: Can the Mecca pact turn its collective defence promise into real support?
articles.summary: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye meet in Islamabad as Houthi attacks on the kingdom continue and Iran talks stay open.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye are meeting in Islamabad on Friday to discuss their Mecca defence pact , as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and sporadic Iranian strikes on other Gulf countries continue.

The officials are meeting for the third time since the three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7 , under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three.

The agreement was signed amid a wider war that began with United States-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told the AFP news agency earlier this week that the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia” – a reference to Yemen, where the Houthis are based – would be on the agenda. He confirmed that the defence and foreign ministers of all three countries would attend the Islamabad meeting.

“Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear,” Asif said.

He described the pact as still being at an early stage.

“Initially we need to have frequent meetings to steer what is being formulated, in a way that in the next couple of months we have everything in place so that we can move forward,” he said.

Pakistan has pledged to defend Saudi territory but has ruled out attacking the Houthis inside Yemen.

Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs set out that boundary on October 9. Spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said Pakistani troops stationed in Saudi Arabia under the alliance would not cross into Yemen to attack the Houthis .

“It is an alliance intended to defend the three countries against aggression,” he said at the weekly news briefing.

On April 11, as Islamabad hosted talks between US and Iranian officials aimed at ending the war, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defence said a Pakistani force , including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz airbase in the country’s Eastern Province under a bilateral mutual defence agreement that Islamabad and Riyadh had signed in 2025.

Muhammad Faisal, a Sydney-based security and foreign policy analyst, said much of the Pakistani military presence in Saudi Arabia rested on that older bilateral arrangement .

“Importantly, Pakistan’s existing military presence and defence coordination with Saudi Arabia largely predate the Mecca Pact,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the bilateral mutual defence pact inked in September 2025, at a time when Gulf countries were reevaluating their dependence on US security guarantees after Israel struck Qatar.

Faisal added that Riyadh had not publicly pressed Islamabad to take part in offensive operations inside Yemen.

But Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies in Riyadh, said that limit fell short of what Saudi Arabia wanted.

Therein lies a dilemma, both for Pakistan and for Saudi Arabia: The deeper Pakistan becomes involved against the Houthis, Karim said, the weaker its diplomatic role would become in US-Iran mediation and in its more recent efforts to mediate between Iran and Saudi Arabia. That’s because Iran is the principal external backer of the Houthis.

“Saudi Arabia wants Pakistan to contribute to its defence against the Houthis, and perhaps to act more against the Houthis in an offensive manner, but it also wants to retain Pakistan as a conduit of diplomatic engagement with Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.

On November 24, the Saudi Civil Defence said 11 people were injured when a tower in Riyadh’s financial centre was hit in a Houthi attack.

At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to Saudi authorities. Twenty-three of them were killed in strikes on airports.

At an emergency meeting of the pact’s member countries in Riyadh on October 5, the committee agreed to provide forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.

The joint statement did not name Yemen or the Houthis.

On November 21, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told Turkish media: “Our current policy is aimed at the defence of Saudi Arabia; no decision has been made on deploying troops inside Yemen. However, the necessary support is being provided in defending Saudi Arabia.”

Omer Ozkizilcik, an Ankara-based analyst and nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, expected the alliance to remain defensive for the moment.

“As of now, as the Saudis only requested defensive support, I do not expect the Mecca Pact to get involved in offensive military operations against the Houthi militias in Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera.

Nawaf Obaid, a senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, outlined the scope of Pakistan’s commitment.

“Pakistan’s military commitment to the defence of Saudi Arabia encompasses capabilities across the land and air domains, including combat aviation, ground formations, integrated air and missile defence, and geospatial intelligence support. Defensive military operations can involve direct combat,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Riyadh meeting was also attended by retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood, a former three-star Pakistani general, who was appointed earlier in September as the alliance’s first secretary-general for a three-year term.

The secretariat is based in Riyadh, where Mahmood met Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud on November 19 to review efforts to build the alliance’s institutional framework, according to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said on October 23 that Islamabad and Riyadh had completed their ratification processes. T urkiye’s parliament approved the agreement on November 5 by 279 votes to 119. On Friday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan signed off on the ratification.

Eyup Ersoy, a visiting research fellow at Pembroke College, University of Oxford, said the alliance had moved quickly.

“The speed and scale of the formation of legal and institutional foundations of the agreement so far attest to the noteworthy performance of the agreement as well,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ozkizilcik, however, pointed to its limits.

“The Mecca Pact does not include a superpower. So, its capabilities and power projections will always be limited, in that it’s an alliance of regional or middle powers,” he said.

The alliance has not publicly detailed how it would decide on a joint military response, which forces it would call on or who would command them.

On October 26 , Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, and Turkiye’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in Tehran.

That meeting is widely believed to have been facilitated by Islamabad. “This showcased Pakistan’s dual role as an active member of the Mecca alliance and a diplomatic bridge between Riyadh and Tehran,” Faisal, the Sydney-based analyst, said.

Obaid said Tehran understood Pakistan’s position.

“Pakistan is not strategically neutral when it comes to Saudi Arabia and Iran, and the Iranians understand this perfectly well. Islamabad has an immediate national security interest in preventing a renewed military confrontation between the United States and Iran, which explains its mediation efforts,” he said.

On October 31, Rezaei told Iranian state television that Prince Khalid had warned that Israel would go after Turkiye once it was done with Iran, and then Saudi Arabia. Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad have not publicly commented on his account.

Javad Heiran-Nia, director of the Persian Gulf Studies Group in Tehran, said Iran viewed the pact through that lens.

“Iran welcomes any mechanism that creates a balance against Israel and weakens the American order in the region,” he told Al Jazeera, even as Tehran “knows that one dimension of the Mecca Pact, and of possible participation in it, is to control Iran and its proxy forces”.

At a weekly briefing on November 20, Pakistani spokesperson Khan said the agreement “is defensive in nature and is not directed against any country”.

The text of the agreement, as submitted to the Turkish parliament , names no country or region as a threat.

Asif declined to tell AFP how the pact would respond to a direct Iranian attack on Saudi Arabia. He named Israel as a possible threat to the region.

“The possibility of some conflict, or aggression from the Israeli side exists, so we need to close our ranks, the countries of this region,” he said.

Karim, from the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies, said pressure on Pakistan could grow if Riyadh’s outreach to Tehran stalled.

“Once Saudi Arabia recognises diplomatic engagement with Iran is not bringing any meaningful outcomes, only then perhaps will it further pressure Pakistan to be more openly involved against the Houthis, which would indeed imperil its goodwill with Iran,” he said.

“The balancing act for Pakistan becomes difficult every day because Iran is unwilling to oblige its concerns and those of Saudi Arabia on Yemen. But for now, it has not crossed a breakdown threshold.”

articles.title: Haryana man books front-row seat and wheelchair assistance for 15-hour Toronto-Delhi flight due to diabetes and leg pain but airline shifts him to middle seat; consumer panel orders Rs 3 lakh compensation
articles.summary: GURGAON: A passenger who was made to endure a 15-hour flight in a middle seat despite paying extra for a front-row allocation on medical grounds has been
articles.body: GURGAON: A passenger who was made to endure a 15-hour flight in a middle seat despite paying extra for a front-row allocation on medical grounds has been awarded Rs 3 lakh compensation by a Haryana consumer commission.The passenger had booked a Delhi-Toronto return ticket for travel in June 2025. Given his diabetes, chronic leg pain and difficulty with mobility, he had specifically opted for a front-row seat on the Toronto-Delhi sector and arranged wheelchair assistance before the journey.But the seating arrangement changed when he arrived to board his return flight. Despite holding a boarding pass showing his confirmed front-row seat, he was assigned a middle-row seat. Airline staff reportedly asked him to accept the revised allocation or get off the aircraft.With limited leave sanctioned for his trip, the passenger continued with the journey. He later complained of worsening leg pain and complications associated with diabetes after reaching India, following which he underwent hospital treatment.His attempts to obtain an explanation and relief from the airline also failed to produce a resolution. After contacting its India-based reservation office by email, he was directed to a general online customer support link.The passenger subsequently approached the consumer commission, seeking Rs 10 lakh in compensation for the alleged deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.The airline disputed the allegations, maintaining that it had returned the Rs 8,799 seat-selection fee to the original payment method in June 2025. It also said an email informing the passenger about the revised seating arrangement had been sent at 3.15 pm on the day of travel. The airline attributed the change to the later wheelchair assistance request and denied any negligence.The commission found that the airline had sufficient notice of the passenger's original booking, which had been made 12 days before departure. It held that any proposed alteration should have been communicated well before the day of travel.The order also pointed out that the airline could not simply change the passenger's allocation without ensuring an appropriate alternative. If the front-row seat was considered unsuitable on safety grounds, it should have arranged another option, such as an aisle or bulkhead seat, keeping his medical and mobility requirements in mind.The commission also rejected the airline's reliance on the refund as a defence. It observed that returning the seat-selection charge after the journey did not compensate for the physical discomfort experienced during the flight or the expenses incurred for subsequent medical treatment.Holding the airline responsible for deficiency in service, the commission ordered it to pay Rs 3 lakh compensation to the passenger within 45 days.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news. articles.title: In the 1860s, Bartholdi imagined a torch-bearing woman at the Suez Canal; the project stalled, but the concept helped inspire America’s Statue of Liberty
articles.summary: Discover how Auguste Bartholdi's original vision of a torch-bearing woman at the Suez Canal in the 1860s laid the groundwork for the iconic Statue of Liberty in America.
articles.body: Most people know the Statue of Liberty from postcards, films, and holiday snaps. Few people know that her story may have begun in Egypt long before New York. Anthropologist Rebecca M. Joseph looked into the monument's early history in a National Park Service report. She found that the design almost certainly grew from an earlier idea. That idea was of a huge torch-bearing woman, which sculptor Auguste Bartholdi imagined as a lighthouse for Egypt’s Suez Canal in the 1860s.A young sculptor who loved big thingsFrédéric-Auguste Bartholdi was born in 1834 in Colmar, France. At the age of 20, he completed his first commission, which was a large bronze statue of a general. He also went to Egypt with a group of French cultural ambassadors. Their job was to photograph some ancient works. According to the National Park Service biography of Bartholdi, they found ruined cities in the desert, but the colossal statues were still standing there. This was what inspired the young artist. Joseph's report also recorded that he drew Egyptian women in 1856, and those sketches would matter later.The lighthouse that never roseBy the late 1860s, the French were building the Suez Canal under the oversight and funding of Egypt's ruler, Khedive Isma’il Pasha. Bartholdi had a meeting with him. He had brought a small figure of a giant lighthouse. It showed an Egyptian peasant woman, or fellah, carrying a torch high to guide ships. Bartholdi called it ‘Egypt (or Progress) Carrying the Light to Asia.’ The khedive turned the design down, and the project stalled. The lighthouse was never built, but the idea did not die there.A new chance in a new countryThe next opportunity came to Bartholdi through Édouard de Laboulaye, a scholar and an abolitionist. Laboulaye suggested the idea of a gift of friendship from France to America. But then war got in the way. During the Franco-Prussian War, Bartholdi led a local regiment to defend his hometown. France lost, and Germany occupied Colmar. He then sailed to America. Soon after arriving in New York Harbour in June 1871, Bartholdi settled on his preferred spot on Bedloe’s Island in New York Harbour. Joseph's report suggested that the statue idea went back to 1870 or 1871. It called the 1865 dinner party story a legend.How much of Egypt is in Lady Liberty?The statue's design, Joseph noted, almost certainly came from Bartholdi’s Egyptian idea. From that earlier plan, he had used his drawings of Egyptian women as models. A note from the park service added that scholars had named the same link. These are both tall women holding a torch high, and both were meant for busy waterways. Certain details did change. The report says Bartholdi replaced a broken shackle and chain in the statue's left hand with tablets marked 4 July 1776. This was what Laboulaye had asked for. The change signalled a message of liberty for all people.A strong link, not a copyThe report used careful words like “almost certainly.” The park service also states that the document’s release didn't mean it endorsed every conclusion in it. The report also tested a popular rumour that Liberty was supposed to be a black woman. However, no evidence was found that Laboulaye or Bartholdi meant that. So the Egyptian connection is a strong one, but it is a connection of designs. It doesn't mean that the statue was copied. The Suez plan may have been a dry run for Bartholdi to imagine a giant woman holding a torch, even though nobody paid for it. The completed statue was assembled in Paris, then disassembled and shipped to America. It was dedicated in 1886 in New York. Today, the Suez design is seen as part of how the Statue of Liberty took shape.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Air Canada changed a passenger’s paid front-row seat to a middle seat despite his medical condition and wheelchair request, forcing him to endure a painful 15-hour Toronto-Delhi flight; consumer court orders airline to pay Rs 3 lakh compensation
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Haryana has directed Air Canada to pay Rs 3 lakh to a passenger after the airline changed his paid front-row
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Haryana has directed Air Canada to pay Rs 3 lakh to a passenger after the airline changed his paid front-row seat to a middle-row seat during an international flight despite his medical condition and wheelchair assistance request. The commission held that the airline was deficient in service and had failed to provide a suitable alternative seat after changing his booking.Why did Air Canada change the passenger's seat?As per the commission order, the complainant, Satish Sharma, a resident of Karnal and a senior government employee, had booked a Delhi-Toronto round-trip ticket with Air Canada. His outward journey was scheduled for June 14, 2025, and the return journey for June 29, 2025.Due to diabetes, chronic leg pain and mobility issues, he paid additional charges for a front-row seat on the return flight and also booked wheelchair assistance.However, while boarding flight AC042 from Toronto to Delhi, the airline shifted him to a middle-row seat without his consent. When he showed his original boarding pass reflecting the front-row seat, the staff reportedly dismissed it as a boarding confusion and told him to either accept the new seat or deboard.With only 15 days of sanctioned leave, Sharma said he had no option but to undertake the 15-hour journey in the middle seat, causing pain and discomfort. After returning to India, he sought medical treatment and alleged that his health had deteriorated.He approached the commission seeking a refund of the upgraded seat fare, Rs 10 lakh as compensation for mental agony, harassment, physical suffering and medical expenses, besides litigation costs.Air Canada denied the allegations, claiming that the seat amount of Rs 8,799 had already been refunded on June 30, 2025. It said Sharma had booked seat 31C before adding his wheelchair assistance request on June 29, and the seat was changed because rows 30 and 31 were emergency exit rows where passengers requiring wheelchair assistance could not be seated.What did the commission say?The bench comprising president Jaswant Singh and members Neeru Agarwal and Sarvjeet Kaur observed that if the airline considered the booked seat unsuitable for a passenger requiring wheelchair assistance, it should have informed him when the request was made so that he could choose another seat."The OP has alleged that the OP has informed the complainant regarding change of seat on 29.06.2025 by sending e-mail i.e. on the day of boarding of flight. Information for change of the seat on the same day of boarding of flight to the complainant, does not fulfill any purpose and is meaningless as at that time the complainant was having no option except to board the flight," the commission observed.It further held that even if the airline had to change the seat for safety reasons, it was its duty to provide a suitable alternative keeping the passenger's health condition in mind. The commission noted that shifting him to a middle seat instead of arranging a suitable seat caused pain, discomfort, harassment and mental agony.It also observed that refunding Rs 8,799 after the journey did not absolve the airline of its responsibility, as the purpose of booking the confirmed seat and wheelchair assistance had been defeated.Final orderAnnounced on October 28, 2026, the commission allowed the complaint and directed Air Canada to:Pay Rs 3 lakh to the complainant towards compensation for mental agony, harassment, physical suffering and medical expenses.Comply with the order within 45 days of receiving a copy.Pay interest at 9 percent per annum on the awarded amount from the date of the order until realisation if it fails to comply within the stipulated period.

articles.title: Gurugram's affluent homebuyers over 55 are rethinking retirement; why Sector 63 is entering conversations about where to spend the winter months
articles.summary: For decades, retirement in India had followed a fairly predictable pattern: people either stayed in their family homes or moved closer to their children
articles.body: For decades, retirement in India had followed a fairly predictable pattern: people either stayed in their family homes or moved closer to their children after stepping away from active work. But that perception is starting to change, especially among wealthy Indians who are approaching or have crossed 55. The question is not only where they will retire, but what kind of life they want to lead in the years ahead.This shift is creating a new opportunity in India’s premium residential market, with Gurugram emerging as an important destination for organised senior living. The newer developments are marketed around independence, convenience, access to healthcare and an active social life, unlike traditional retirement facilities. Buyers want thoughtfully designed homes, barrier-free spaces, wellness amenities, housekeeping support and communities where they can stay socially connected without giving up the comforts of a high-end lifestyle.The entry of big real estate developers in this segment is adding momentum. One such example is DLF’s launch of The Aureva in Gurugram’s Sector 63, which is its first dedicated senior-living project. The development has reportedly clocked sales of around ₹1,985 crore with an average ticket size of around ₹11.5 crore which shows the buying power of this emerging buyer category.The interest is also coming amid changing urban realities. Some older residents and families are rethinking where they spend the colder months, as the NCR’s winter pollution has become a regular feature. Access to hospitals, more planned residential surroundings, green spaces and connectivity are increasingly part of these conversations.It is too early to say if micro markets like Sector 63 will become winter addresses of choice for older homebuyers, but the trend is worth watching. Retirement accommodation is slowly shedding the stereotype of a premium residential option for those who want to stay independent, comfortable and connected as they age.The broader numbers support the attention this corridor is receiving. According to Cushman & Wakefield, in the third quarter of 2026, Gurugram accounted for 77% of all new residential launches in Delhi-NCR, with Golf Course Extension alone contributing 21% of the quarter’s supply, the second-highest submarket after New Gurgaon. Gurugram also drove 78% of luxury-segment launches in the same period, and the luxury category itself saw a 71% jump from the previous quarter. Weighted launch prices in the high-end and luxury segments rose 24% and 21% year-on-year respectively, while Gurugram’s luxury rentals recorded the highest annual growth in NCR at 4%.Across Delhi-NCR, the same pattern is becoming clearer. Gurugram has emerged as the main market for organised senior living because of its mix of healthcare access, airport connectivity and a large base of affluent households. Demand is coming both from local families and from NRIs buying for parents, while several developers have entered the segment in the last 12–18 months. Average ticket sizes have stayed high, and consultants say the category still has low penetration relative to the number of households with members above 60."We are witnessing more buyers over 55, choosing a home based on the life it offers. They want green space nearby, good hospitals, a community around them and easy access to the rest of the city. Most of them want to stay active and independent, and they don't want to give up the comforts they're used to. That's why areas like Sector 63 on Golf Course Extension Road are drawing attention. It's close to the Aravallis, the infrastructure is improving, and the social amenities are already in place," says Aakash Ohri, Managing Director & Chief Business Officer, DLF Home Developers.At the core, these senior living formats are anchored around health, wellness and holistic well being. Such developments are supported by on call and in house medical assistance, 24/7 ambulance availability, and senior centric design elements including barrier free walkways, supported corridors, accessible washrooms, anti slip flooring, and appropriately planned fitness and common spaces. A strong focus is also placed on fostering a sense of community, enabling social interaction, reducing isolation, and creating environments where seniors feel secure, engaged and at home.Shalin Raina, Managing Director, Residential Services, Cushman & Wakefield, says, " A small but growing set of developers is addressing senior living requirements through dedicated projects or by earmarking portions within larger residential developments. These homes are primarily designed for end use, with a clear emphasis on ease of living. In parallel, some established players are adopting an asset light approach by leasing residential buildings and retrofitting them with age appropriate designs, specialised fit outs and curated amenities, supported by integrated services such as housekeeping, laundry and in house dining for a hassle free living experience."Not a pollution free zone thoughIt is obvious that Sector 63 is not being marketed as a pollution-free residential destination and it would be misleading to suggest that the area is insulated from Gurugram’s wider air-quality problems. Golf Course Extension Road continues to be troubled with road-dust pollution especially during construction activity, heavy traffic and dry weather. The city is also still struggling with extended spells of bad air- especially during the winter months, when the pollution levels remain high for weeks at a time.What does seem to be changing, however, is how some senior homebuyers and their families are assessing residential sites. They are beginning to look more closely at individual sectors, neighbourhoods and stretches rather than treating Golf Course Extension Road as a continuous residential corridor. But people who track such preferences say the conversation increasingly is about finding relatively better local surroundings in a city that continues to face significant environmental issues. For some senior buyers even small differences in the immediate neighbourhood such as greenery, traffic flow, construction activity and nature of surrounding development can influence their decision.At the same time, these buyers are not necessarily looking to abandon urban amenities or adopt a quieter, more isolated way of life. The ability to reach social, cultural and commercial hubs, connectivity to central Gurugram, easy access to the airport and proximity to healthcare facilities continue to be important considerations. Many seniors today are active and independent, and they want to continue to have access to the infrastructure and conveniences to which they have become accustomed. They don’t want to disconnect from the city, but rather find a residential environment that offers a relatively better balance between accessibility, everyday comfort and local surroundings.In two or three winters, it will be evident if this emerging preference will lead to sustained demand for Sector 63. As more homes hit the market and buyers become more aware of the seasonal performance of various neighbourhoods, the variances between individual micro-markets could become more pronounced. Sector 63 is currently one of the few places along this corridor where the conversation on local environmental conditions, senior-friendly living and urban connectivity appears to be gaining traction. The real test will be if this perception translates into real home buying decisions in terms of consistently better on-ground conditions.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: ‘Borrowing to make ends meet’: The rising cost of living in Europe
articles.summary: Prices are climbing again across Europe as energy costs surge.
articles.body:
As winter closes in, millions of people across Europe are bracing for another season of rising bills, tighter budgets and hard choices at home.

Inflation in the eurozone has climbed to its highest level in three years, as conflict in the Middle East disrupts oil and gas supplies and drives up energy prices, pushing up the cost of everything from heating to the weekly food shop.

In Athens, Giorgos*, a 40-year-old journalist and father of an 11-year-old, says his salary has risen from 800 euros ($878) to 1,100 euros ($1,208) a month over the past two years, but he has not felt the raise.

“Just as before, I’m still borrowing money just to make ends meet,” he said. Even a gyros souvlaki sandwich, long considered Greece’s “people’s food”, now costs more than 4 euros, he added.

His experience is shared across much of Europe, where prices are rising again after two years of relative calm. Inflation in the eurozone has doubled from 2 percent in December 2025 to 4 percent in October 2026, its highest level in three years.

Energy has been the biggest driver, with energy inflation rising to 21 percent in October, its highest level since December 2022, when it was 25.5 percent in the first winter after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Eurostat.

Energy prices have risen far faster than any other category and are pushing up the cost of transport, heating and food.

According to the European Central Bank (ECB) Lithuania (6.1 percent), Bulgaria (5.9 percent) and Greece (5.7 percent) now have the highest inflation rates in the eurozone, adding pressure on households already among the most stretched in the region.

Inflation in Cyprus jumped from 0.1 percent at the end of last year to 5.4 percent, and in Italy from 1.2 percent to 5.6 percent.

Prices have also accelerated quickly in Belgium, where inflation rose from 2.2 percent to 5.2 percent, and in France, where it rose from 0.7 percent to 3.7 percent.

A handful of countries have bucked the trend. Between December 2025 and October 2026, inflation has eased in Slovakia (from 4.1 percent to 2.9 percent), Estonia (3.6 percent), Latvia (3.1), Austria (3.5) and Malta (2.3), setting Lithuania apart from its Baltic neighbours.

The current rise is still well below the peak that followed the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, but for many families it is a second shock before they have fully recovered from the first.

How much more expensive has life become?

In North London, Emma*, 33, who works in corporate governance and lives alone, says the cost of food and bills keeps rising, with rent “the biggest killer”.

She has cancelled streaming subscriptions and switched to a cheaper brand of cat food for her pet cat after the one she always purchased started putting less in each can at a higher price.

She now sees her friends less, because nearly 10 pounds ($13) for a return Tube journey is “ridiculous”.

“I think this is detrimental to our mental health and has exacerbated the loneliness epidemic,” she said.

She’s not alone in feeling she has to make choices to survive. This squeeze is being felt across Europe.

According to Eurostat , a typical basket of goods and services such as food, housing, energy and transport now costs 69 percent more than it did in 2000, and around two-fifths of that increase has come in just the past four years.

The sharpest rise came in 2022, when prices jumped by more than 8 percent in a single year as energy costs soared after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The steepest increases have been in Central and Eastern Europe.

Prices in Hungary have more than tripled since 2000, meaning the goods and services that cost 100 euros ($115) in 2000 now cost about 335 Euros ($385), with a surge of 17 percent in 2023 alone. Estonia and Latvia are not far behind.

Finding work in Europe is far easier than it was a decade ago, but in many countries it has been getting harder again since 2022.

According to Eurostat , southern Europe has seen the biggest turnaround.

At the height of the eurozone debt crisis in 2013, unemployment reached 27.8 percent in Greece and 26.1 percent in Spain, meaning more than a quarter of people looking for work could not find a job.

Unemployment in both countries has fallen steadily since then as their economies recovered, to 8.9 percent in Greece and 10.5 percent in Spain in 2025, although Spain still has the highest rate in the EU.

The picture has shifted in northern Europe, where unemployment has risen since 2022 as economies slowed.

Unemployment in Finland has climbed to 9.7 percent in 2025, giving it the second-highest jobless rate in the bloc, ahead of Greece (8.9 percent) and Sweden (8.8 percent).

How much room do governments have to help?

When prices rise, people often look to their governments for financial support. But how much help a government can provide depends partly on how much debt it already carries.

The debt-to-GDP ratio compares a country’s total government debt with the value of everything its economy produces in a year. A ratio of 100 percent means the government owes as much as the economy produces in a year. The higher the ratio, the more money the government may have to spend on interest payments, leaving less available to help households.

Emma believes governments are spending in the wrong places. “Stop using taxpayer money to subsidise high energy bills while fossil fuel and grid companies continue making record profits,” she said, calling for windfall tax loopholes to be closed so those profits fund household relief directly.

According to data from International Monetary Fund (IMF) , Italy and Greece carry the heaviest debts in Europe, each owing well over a year’s worth of economic output.

France, Ukraine, Belgium and the UK also owe more than their economies produce in a year.

At the other end of the scale, Estonia, Denmark and Luxembourg owe relatively little, giving them far more room to respond.

Several of the countries with the highest inflation, including Greece, Italy and Belgium, are also among the most indebted, leaving them with the least room to cushion the blow.

Education and healthcare: What governments are choosing to spend on.

In Belgium, Maya*, a university lecturer in her 50s, is searching for student housing for her daughter, who starts university next year.

“It used to be you could get a place, no problem, for 300 euros,” she said. “One of my neighbours just told me she paid 900 a month for her kid.”

She says more of her students now commute an hour or more to get to class, which she finds “undemocratic” because it shapes who can afford to live near campus.

In France , where student protests over overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages have grown into a nationwide movement, high school student Marius Mesnil told Al Jazeera that conditions in schools have deteriorated year after year.

“With every budget, there are fewer teachers,” he said.

Across Europe, how much governments spend on schools and hospitals shows what they are prioritising, and how much support they can give people as costs rise.

Sweden and Iceland spend the most on education in Europe, while spending has stayed largely unchanged in most Western European countries since 2016.

Denmark is a notable exception, with spending falling sharply over the period.

Many countries in Eastern Europe have increased their spending, including Slovakia, Bulgaria and Lithuania. Some of the countries carrying the heaviest debts, including Greece and Italy, are among those spending the least on education.

Healthcare spending rose across Europe during the COVID-19 pandemic and has since fallen back in most countries, though it remains higher than before the pandemic in most of them.

Austria now spends the most, at 9.5 percent of its GDP in 2024, followed by Czechia and Croatia (9 percent each) and France (8.9 percent).

As temperatures drop, people are finding ways to stay warm without turning up the heating. Emma in London has bought a heated blanket so she does not need to heat her whole flat, and says she has had to put food and water before heating.

In Belgium, Maya’s family move around the house in wearable blankets; her daughters sleep with hot water bottles.

In Athens, Giorgos plans to keep his heater to a minimum and stock up on rugs, blankets and fleeces, admitting there have been winters when he had to choose between heating and food.

The worry never lifts. “Anxiety is something of a constant,” he said. “It doesn’t go away – if anything, it’s only intensifying now.”

*Names have been changed at the interviewees’ request to protect their identities.

articles.title: Strobe Talbott, deputy secretary of state, has died
articles.summary: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday.
articles.body: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80. His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home. The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964. Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine. After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton. Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration’s approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter’s nuclear tests in 1998. “Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure,” said Clinton in a statement after Talbott’s death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev’s memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton’s job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, “somehow, I got the better end of the deal.” Both he and Hillary were “deeply saddened” by the passing of “a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being,” he said. Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board. Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled “Our Founders’ Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump,” which was published in 2020. He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren. His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

articles.title: Test results from samples taken after Iowa detonation are expected soon, EPA says
articles.summary: Test results from sampling done following the U.S. Army’s detonation of a stockpile of lead azide in Iowa are expected to start coming in as early as Friday, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
articles.body: LITTLE ROCK, Ark. — Test results from sampling done following the U.S. Army’s detonation of a stockpile of lead azide in Iowa are expected to start coming in as early as Friday, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. EPA personnel and contractors took over 1,500 samples of air, water, soil and dust before the detonation of the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives. After the detonation, they took hundreds of samples including from homes, parks and drinking water, the EPA said in a Thursday statement. Samples were sent to labs for testing, the EPA said. “The Trump EPA will continue its presence on the ground for as long as needed to ensure the proper environmental monitoring is taking place following the successful controlled detonation,” the agency said. The EPA said there continued to be “zero” airborne lead detected in the region since Wednesday’s controlled detonation. In addition to lead exposure, the EPA also is testing for other compounds that could have been released in the explosion. “The agency is testing for everything we were anticipating could potentially be released as a result of the controlled detonation,” the EPA said. The Army has said detonating the stockpile was the safest option because it was degrading and might explode uncontrollably as the weather got colder.
